title: Material Systems Research Matrix
subtitle: A heuristic map of digital–physical discourse and system openness in material systems research
framing: This matrix is a heuristic and interpretive map, not a fixed taxonomy. It positions research by the degree of digital–physical discourse it establishes and the degree to which the material system is treated as closed and bounded or open and ecologically entangled. The map is intended to make visible where research clusters, where gaps remain, and how different projects frame material interaction, control, and exchange. i.e. a designerly orientation map for locating gaps, tendencies, and possible research territories.

x.name: Digital–physical discourse
x.description: How explicitly and continuously digital systems maintain feedback, update, or coupling relationships with material behaviour.

y.name: System openness
y.description: How far the material system is treated as bounded and controllable versus open to exchange, ecological entanglement, and ongoing transformation.

bottom_left.title: Closed systems with low discourse
bottom_left.description: Material systems treated as bounded artefacts with little or no meaningful digital–material coupling.

bottom_right.title: Closed systems with high discourse
bottom_right.description: Material systems with strong digital–material interaction, but organised within bounded and predefined conditions to guide or control a desired output.

top_left.title: Open systems with low discourse
top_left.description: Systems embedded in wider contextual or ecological exchange, but with limited or no explicit digital participation.

top_right.title: Open systems with high discourse
top_right.description: Systems in which digital tools participate meaningfully in evolving, context-dependent, and ecologically entangled material processes.

questions.text: Does the digital system maintain explicit feedback or update relationships with the material system?
Is the material system treated as bounded and controllable, or as evolving and ecologically entangled?
Are the relationships between input, stimulus, and response predefined and stabilised, or expected to change over time?
Does the research focus on the designed artefact alone, or on its wider relations with context, landscape, or ecology?
Does the system support return, decay, renewal, or replenishment, or does it primarily optimise a desired response?
